messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 47

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Julian was twenty-one when he returned from three months as a relief worker in a fractured Middle Eastern province. He had traveled with a humanitarian coalition, carrying medical supplies and water purification tablets to displaced families. On his final week, the convoy route shifted without warning, and the compound where his team distributed aid came under sudden fire. In the chaos, voices rose in rapid, sharp Arabic from nearby rooftops and alleys. Men in uniforms and civilians alike sprinted past his position, their movements jerking and unpredictable. When a stranger’s hand brushed Julian’s shoulder while directing him toward cover, Julian froze, certain he was being singled out. The explosion that followed left a ringing silence and a scene so violent, so absolute, that it felt impossible. He had come to believe, in the weeks that followed, that the story of what happened that day could not possibly be true. Yet there he was, standing in the dust, the terror exactly as it had been, refusing to fade into memory. Back in his hometown, Julian took a position at a local Social Ministry, helping newly resettled families navigate housing applications and legal paperwork. The work demanded patience, but his nervous system no longer recognized ordinary surroundings as safe. Conversations at the center’s break room about the war quickly became unbearable; the moment a colleague mentioned military strategy or equipment, Julian’s pulse spiked and he would step out into the hallway until his breathing steadied. Even hearing Arabic shouted on a television screen or in the street beside him sent him into immediate guard. He could not separate the past from the present when recalling the incident. Sitting alone in his apartment, trying to tell his wife what had happened was as impossible as walking back into the compound. The words felt like opening a valve, flooding his body with the same panic he had experienced in the moment. Strangers in the grocery store or approaching him on the sidewalk were no longer just people; they were potential threats. He found himself tensing the instant a hand gestured toward him or someone stepped forward to ask for directions. Over months, his routines shifted in parallel, each habit carving deeper into his days. He delayed sleep, staying up until 3 a.m. to read or pace. Nights were broken by sudden awakenings; he would stand in the hallway, checking every lock, every window, until his fingers were numb and his breathing slowed. He ruminated relentlessly on how the incident could have been prevented. If only he had suggested a different supply route, if only he had spoken louder to his team leader, if only he had positioned himself differently, the outcome would not have been so irreversible. The guilt of those counterfactuals settled over him as a constant companion. Joyful moments grew difficult to inhabit. When the ministry team planned a weekend retreat, Julian declined, telling himself that letting himself feel hope would be disrespectful to what he had witnessed. He stopped looking at photographs of his deployment, avoiding any situation that might make him feel happy or hopeful, as though positivity required a betrayal of the event. At his office visit, Julian sat across from a clinician, his hands folded tightly in his lap. The ministry had noticed his absences, his distracted posture during client sessions, the way he flinched when a coworker reached for a file folder too quickly. He had come to this room because his wife gently but firmly told him he could no longer carry the isolation alone, and because he could no longer explain why he checked the doorframe three times before leaving for work. He was afraid that seeking help meant opening the same floodgates, that speaking aloud would make the terror permanent. Yet, beneath the fear, he hoped that someone might help him understand why his body still answered the world like a battlefield, and perhaps, just perhaps, allow him to live in the present again without feeling like an imposter in his own life.
